body: . Aluminium, copper, steel, graphite and critical minerals are all seeing stronger consumption as data centre construction and power infrastructure expand across the US. Supply constraints are amplifying price pressures.

Tight availability of metals such as indium, gallium, graphite and steel feedstocks is pushing prices higher as demand from AI infrastructure accelerates. Power infrastructure is emerging as a critical growth driver. Beyond data centres themselves, demand for transmission networks, substations, cooling systems and energy storage is creating significant new opportunities across multiple metals markets.
AI and data centers create a new metals demand cycle
Metals producers across the US are now seeing demand spikes for metals ranging from aluminium to indium, and
will be a driving force in the years to come.
Metals markets have shifted to capture the growing demand from the data center industry, but pressures on the demand side and tight supply for some metals have led to a sharp increase in prices.

Demand will strengthen further as AI demand ramps up globally, and the ever-changing metals industry will continue to see a shift in traditional demand sources as the data center industry continues to grow in the US.
Data centers drive up aluminium demand, producers say

The relationship between aluminium and data centers is complex, as primary aluminium smelters and data centers consume large amounts of electricity. However, products and materials consisting of primary and secondary aluminium are used throughout data centers.
products in the US, Hydro Aluminium Metals USA president Duncan Pitchford told Fastmarkets.

Pitchford is also head of recycling for North America and head of commercial for the Americas.  Aluminium is used in several applications across data center development, including cooling management systems, racking and enclosure for servers, and power distribution.
Aluminium gains share in power transmission and cooling systems

When compared to the superior electrical conductor copper, aluminium offers both weight savings and a cost advantage, leading to the use of aluminium busbar to conduct and distribute electricity within switchgear, panelboards and power systems.  Overhead power cables linking the US utility network use aluminium wire, according to the Aluminum Association. Aluminium is the “preferred material” for electricity transmission and distribution uses, due to its lower weight and price.  As electricity demand continues to grow, demand for power transmission and distribution infrastructure will strengthen.  Aluminium has high thermal conductivity and is used in heat sinks and cooling systems used in thermal management.  As data centers have transitioned to closed-loop systems, thermal management applications like cooling towers and large-scale heating, ventilation and air conditioning (HVAC) equipment are a source of demand, Pitchford said.  HVAC equipment manufacturers are increasing the use of aluminium over copper, and Hydro is a pioneer in this area, Pitchford said.  Additionally, wiring requires a home, Pitchford said. Cable trays and conduits used to house wiring are also made from aluminium.  “Hydro is the largest manufacturer of seamless aluminium tubing in the US, and we see demand growth from data center applications, particularly for larger-diameter conduit,” Pitchford said.
Domestic sourcing gains importance for US customers
Additionally, Pitchford said customers asked Hydro to supply recycled materials produced in the US.

“We have seen an increased interest from customers in domestically produced material to reduce supply chain risk … and replace supply previously sourced from the Middle East to manufacture cable tray,” Pitchford said.   A Prysmian spokesperson also confirmed increased demand from data centers. The spokesperson said the company has seen “a lot of demand” from data centers in the US for its cable products, produced using aluminium.   In an August 2026 earnings call, Century Aluminum executives reported seeing strong demand in the US, driven in part by investments in power and data infrastructure.

The red metal is ubiquitous in data center infrastructure, used in everything from power distribution to grounding and utility interconnections, transformers, battery energy storage, cooling infrastructure, and more.  “Copper forms the backbone of the AI infrastructure, offering unmatched electrical and thermal conductivity, thus enabling data centers to distribute power and manage heat efficiently while minimizing resistive losses,” Olga Savina, senior analyst at Fitch Solutions’ Commodities at BMI, told Fastmarkets.  “It’s also important to recognize that a significant amount of copper demand occurs outside the data center itself. Many AI campuses require new transmission connections, substations, feeders, transformers, and other utility upgrades before the facility can even be energized,” Paul Charles, chief executive officer of Charles & Associates; creator of the Full Stack Data Centers™ Platform; and co-chair of NAATBatt ESS & Data Center Community told Fastmarkets.
Power infrastructure drives demand beyond the data centre campus

According to the Copper Development Association, modern liquid-cooled data centers require 20-40 tonnes of copper per megawatt of applied power. Charles and Savina both agree with this estimate, though Charles noted that this is a planning range rather than a fixed industry value. In 2024, Macquarie also estimated that between 330,000 and 420,000 tonnes of copper will be used in data centers by 2030.  While it’s been a topic of rising interest both within and outside of the mining industry over the last few years, the challenge in forecasting AI infrastructure is in the rapidly evolving technology.

“That’s the part of the story I think often gets overlooked,” he said.
“Only a few years ago, enterprise data centers typically operated at relatively modest rack power levels. Today’s

Those changes affect electrical distribution, cooling infrastructure, and ultimately copper demand,” Charles told Fastmarkets.  “While not acting as the sole rationale behind the copper price performance in 2026 thus far, AI-driven sentiment is expected to continue to shape, if not dominate, the narrative,” Savina said.
Pressure mounts for already tight US critical minerals market

Indium phosphide, a combination of indium metal and phosphorus, is used to make lasers and optical components used in fiber optic networks throughout data centers.  Indium’s primary use is in LCD screens, but indium is used throughout data centers as well. Right now, buyers are not finding it difficult to source indium for data center needs, one source said, but supply concerns over indium’s possible addition to China’s export control list have put upward pressure on US indium prices.  Indium 99.99%, ddp US was assessed at $840-890 per kg on Friday August 21, rising by almost 10% since July 10, when the assessment was $770-810 per kg.  Another critical mineral, gallium nitride, is “a wide-bandgap semiconductor material used in a growing list of high-voltage applications,” according to Texas Instruments in a 2023 blog post. Gallium nitride is valuable to data centers because of its power density and energy efficiency and is used in a variety of applications.  Another gallium compound, gallium oxide, is used in semiconductors. A spike in gallium oxide demand has pushed US gallium metal prices higher in recent months.  Fastmarkets assessed Gallium 99.99%, ddp US at $3,000-3,300 per kg August 21, flat from August 7 but up by 1.61% from July 10 and up by 15.89% from June 26.  Prices of gallium are expected to rise further because “China is purposely holding back [gallium and germanium, another critical mineral used in data centers] from the West to slow down [US] AI data centers,” a seller source explained.
Graphite demand shifts from EVs to data centres

As a result, some producers seeking to establish a supply chain in the US have pivoted from the electric vehicle sector to batteries for data centers. Data center demand, coupled with rising defense industry demand and the desire to reduce dependence on Chinese graphite imports, has led to a surge in graphite projects in the US recently.
Additionally, AI could boost output, but rising demand threatens to further restrict the supply of critical minerals.   While

AIMinr founder Ari Rostami and co-founder Dela Rostami said rising AI demand could be a “double-edged sword” for critical minerals.  “There’s a huge demand for the critical minerals, and data centers are actually [having a] compounding effect on the demand,” Ari Rostami explained in a June interview with Fastmarkets.
Finished steel demand rises from AI amid constricted US steel market

Data center construction projects are also having an impact on finished steel demand, including hot-rolled coil, beams, structural steel, tubing, rebar, and wire rod. For example, publicly available data show that data-center construction starts accounted for more than 20% of all non-residential building starts between May 2025 and May 2026.  These demand drivers are further exacerbating what some sources have described as a shortage of hot-rolled coil (HRC), a key feedstock used to produce hollow structural sections.  As of the time of publication, numerous mills are not offering HRC on spot terms.  Sources have also said that those with contracts are being held to their contractual minimums, with at least one mill telling customers that if they want to purchase HRC beyond their contract minimums, they will need to do so on the spot market.  A Midwest structural tube market participant told Fastmarkets that their company has seen strong demand from data center projects, adding that their ability to fulfill orders is being hindered by the monthslong tightness in HRC supply.
Long products emerge as key beneficiaries of AI investment

“We’ll get a run on tube [orders] to make structures, cabinets, server racks – they can’t get it fast enough. We can’t keep up,” they said. “As soon as we add the equipment and the people [needed to meet our customers’ demand], we’ll run out of [HRC]. I don’t know how we’re going to keep up at this point. [Orders just keep] coming in faster than we can produce it.”  The source also relayed that they attempted to purchase more than 2,000 short tons of spot market HRC from a domestic producer at the start of July but were told the mill could fulfill only 10% of the order.  The availability of galvanized sheet has been “extremely tight, with data center demand chewing up mill availability,” a Midwest distributor said. Construction industry buyers are bypassing distributors and buying these products directly from the mills.  Data centers appear to be adding a low-single-digit percentage lift to overall US steel demand, based on construction industry analysts and surveys. However, data centers are providing a much more meaningful lift to selected long products – especially beams, structural sections, rebar, fabricated rebar and some merchant-bar applications.  Structural steel, including joists, beams and decking, is central to data center construction. Foundations and heavy floor loads require reinforcing steel, and some mills have highlighted their modular rebar systems for these structural support applications.  US steelmakers face a ‘robust opportunity’ in data center expansion, according to Barry Zekelman, executive chairman and chief executive officer of Zekelman Industries.

The potential global capital expenditure in data center expansion from now until 2030 was estimated at $3 trillion, according to Jones Lang LaSalle (JLL), a Chicago-based firm specializing in commercial real estate and investment management.  In a report released earlier this year, JLL forecast that the global data center sector would “effectively double in size” and grow from 97 gigawatts (GW) in 2025 to 200 GW in 2030, with growth in the Americas rising from 49 GW to 109 GW.
